title: Add `dual_contour` (DC+QEF) mesh extraction op
abstract:
# Add `dual_contour` (DC + QEF) mesh extraction op ## Overview Adds `dual_contour`, a CUDA dual-contouring surface mesher that turns a narrow-band signed distance field on an OnIndex grid into a triangle mesh, alongside the existing `marching_cubes`. It composes directly with the `reinitialize_sdf` / `rebuild_narrow_band` ops, which produce exactly the kind of clean narrow-band SDF it consumes. The op is built on the batch's cached NanoVDB VoxelBlockManagers (VBM, `GridBatchData::vbm()` from #747): the $3 \times 3 \times 3$ box stencil is decoded once per voxel and reused by every downstream stage. The whole batch is meshed together, so host syncs and kernel launches do not grow with the number of grids (see [Batched execution](#batched-execution)). It returns `(vertices, faces, normals)` as three `JaggedTensor`s jagged over the grid batch — vertices and normals are `float32` of shape `[B, -1, 3]`, faces are `int64` of shape `[B, -1, 3]` with grid-local indices, and normals are the normalized SDF gradient at each vertex. ## Algorithm For each cube cell whose 8 corners are all active and straddle the isovalue, one vertex is placed by minimizing a quadratic error function (QEF) over the 12 edge zero-crossings $\mathbf{p}_i$ and their interpolated gradient normals $\mathbf{n}_i$: $$E(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i \big[\, \mathbf{n}_i \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}_i) \,\big]^2 .$$ Geometrically each term is the squared distance to the tangent plane at a crossing, so the minimizer best-fits all of them and snaps onto sharp features that a plain crossing-average would round off. Setting $\partial E / \partial \mathbf{x} = 0$ gives the $3 \times 3$ normal equations $$A\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}, \qquad A = \sum_i \mathbf{n}_i \mathbf{n}_i^{\top}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \sum_i \mathbf{n}_i \,(\mathbf{n}_i \cdot \mathbf{p}_i),$$ solved with a closed-form symmetric solve, re-centred on the crossing centroid and Tikhonov-regularized for stability in flat / underconstrained cells. Connectivity is the dual of marching cubes: for each sign-changing minimal grid edge, the 4 cells sharing that edge each contribute their vertex to one quad; quads are split into triangles and oriented outward by the SDF gradient. Triangle output is deterministic (per-cell count -> cumsum -> write), and unreferenced vertices are pruned. Optional cluster-collapse decimation: `reduce = F` collapses uniform $F \times F \times F$ index-space blocks of surface cells to a single QEF-solved vertex each ($\sim F^2$ fewer vertices); `adaptivity` keeps feature cells at full detail and only collapses "flat" coarse blocks (those whose cells' edge normals are well aligned). Connectivity merges for free, since quads referencing cells that collapsed to the same vertex become degenerate and are dropped. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["narrow-band SDF on a grid batch
(grouped into chunks of consecutive grids)"] --> B["gatherFusedKernel: one VBM decode/voxel, all grids of the chunk
→ neighbour table + gradient + surface flag + coord"] B --> C["compact surface cells (+ each cell's grid)"] C --> D{"decimate?"} D -- "reduce = 1, adaptivity = 0" --> E["QEF: one vertex per surface cell"] D -- "reduce / adaptivity" --> F["cluster cells (keys disjoint per grid)
→ one merged QEF vertex per cluster"] E --> G["connectivity: quad per sign-changing minimal edge
→ triangles, oriented by the SDF gradient"] F --> G G --> H["prune unreferenced vertices, rebase faces to grid-local indices,
normalise normals"] H --> I["(vertices, faces, normals) JaggedTensors"] ``` ## Relationship to OpenVDB `VolumeToMesh` This follows the dual-contouring approach of OpenVDB's `tools/VolumeToMesh.h`, but is a leaner VBM-native reimplementation that diverges in two deliberate ways: it places vertices by a QEF least-squares solve (classic Dual Contouring) rather than by averaging the edge crossings (the "mass point" `VolumeToMesh` uses by default), and it decimates by simple cluster-collapse rather than `VolumeToMesh`'s seam-stitched octree region merge. It does not reproduce `VolumeToMesh`'s marching-cubes-style ambiguous-cell handling or its quad output (we always triangulate). For the watertight, smooth, isotropic narrow-band SDFs this op targets, these simplifications are reasonable. ## References (cited in the source) - T. Ju, F. Losasso, S. Schaefer, J. Warren, "Dual Contouring of Hermite Data", ACM TOG 21(3) / SIGGRAPH 2002 — the core method (QEF vertex placement on edge Hermite data, dual connectivity, octree adaptive simplification our decimation is a simplified form of). - M. Garland, P. Heckbert, "Surface Simplification Using Quadric Error Metrics", SIGGRAPH 1997 — the quadric error metric $A = \sum_i \mathbf{n}_i \mathbf{n}_i^{\top}$ that the vertex placement minimizes. - L. Kobbelt, M. Botsch, U. Schwanecke, H.-P. Seidel, "Feature Sensitive Surface Extraction from Volume Data", SIGGRAPH 2001 — placing the vertex at the intersection of the edge-crossing tangent planes. - W. Lorensen, H. Cline, "Marching Cubes: A High Resolution 3D Surface Construction Algorithm", SIGGRAPH 1987 — the sign-based isosurface extraction that dual contouring is the dual of. ## Batched execution `dual_contour` meshes the grids of a batch together rather than looping over them. Consecutive grids are grouped into chunks of at most $2^{22}$ active voxels (a larger grid forms its own chunk), and each chunk runs the pipeline above once: - One gather launch decodes every grid's voxels through the batch's VBM (`VoxelBlockManagerBatchView` maps each VBM block to its grid). Slots are chunk-wide and slot 0 is the shared background; the box stencil never leaves its grid, so connectivity never crosses grids. - Surface cells come out sorted by slot and hence grouped by grid. A `searchsorted` over the batch's voxel offsets gives each cell's grid, which selects its world transform. - Decimation keys are offset into a disjoint per-grid key range (per-grid origins and spans come from a warp-aggregated bounds kernel), so clusters never span grids. - After the vertex prune, faces are rebased onto grid-local vertex indices. Each grid's output is identical to meshing that grid alone: bitwise without decimation, and with decimation the vertex and face counts and faces match, with only the order of the double-atomic cluster sums differing. A chunk costs a constant 3 host syncs (surface compaction, triangle count, vertex prune), and assembling the outputs costs none, plus 1 or 2 cluster relabels when decimating, and about 89 bytes of scratch per voxel (about 370 MB at the chunk cap). Timings against the earlier per-grid loop, on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (idle). Dense cubes with a sphere SDF; each entry is the median of 15 calls, the faster of two interleaved runs: | batch | full detail | `reduce=4` | `adaptivity=0.5` | |---|---|---|---| | 64 × 17³ | 25.9 → 0.56 ms (46×) | 37.9 → 0.89 ms (43×) | 56.2 → 1.15 ms (49×) | | 16 × 33³ | 7.07 → 0.59 ms (12×) | 9.96 → 0.92 ms (11×) | 13.9 → 1.18 ms (12×) | | 4 × 65³ | 2.14 → 0.66 ms (3.2×) | 2.87 → 1.00 ms (2.9×) | 3.93 → 1.25 ms (3.1×) | | 1 × 129³ | 1.04 → 0.73 ms (1.4×) | 1.18 → 1.06 ms (1.1×) | 1.46 → 1.33 ms (1.1×) | The pruning step flags referenced vertices and numbers them with a cumsum, where it used to run a sort-based `unique_dim`. The outputs are built from per-grid offsets with the unchecked JaggedTensor constructor, so a call no longer syncs to validate them. Together these cut a full-detail call on a single chunk from 13 to 3 host syncs. ## Public API and wiring - `Grid.dual_contour(field, iso=0.0, reduce=1, adaptivity=0.0)` and `GridBatch.dual_contour(...)`. - Functional entrypoints `fvdb.functional.dual_contour_single` / `dual_contour_batch`. - pybind binding `_fvdb_cpp.dual_contour` and the corresponding `.pyi` stub. - `src/fvdb/detail/ops/DualContour.{h,cu}`, added to the CUDA build in `src/CMakeLists.txt`. ## Tests `tests/unit/test_dc.py` covers both validity and analytic ground truth: - Valid closed genus-0 mesh on a sphere SDF: in-range non-degenerate triangles, no boundary or non-manifold edges, and Euler characteristic $V - E + F = 2$. - Analytic planar SDF reproduced exactly: interior vertices lie on the plane $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d + \mathrm{iso}$ and carry the plane normal $\mathbf{n}$ to float precision (QEF reproduces planes exactly). - Sphere radius / normals: every vertex within a sub-voxel band of the analytic radius, with radial normals. - Composition with `reinitialize_sdf` and `rebuild_narrow_band(pad=True)`. - Extent agreement with `marching_cubes` (cross-implementation sanity check). - Batch-vs-single parity on the non-decimated path. - Batched execution: each grid's slice is bitwise equal to meshing it alone. This covers mixed grid sizes, a grid with no surface, an empty grid, 24 small grids, a batch spanning several $2^{22}$-voxel chunks, and a sliced `GridBatch` view. - Decimation never merges clusters across grids. A batch of identical, overlapping grids must decimate each grid exactly as it would alone; disabling the per-grid key bases makes this test fail. - Decimation bounds (`reduce=4` strictly fewer vertices; `adaptivity=0.5` non-empty, no more than full detail). - Empty-surface case returns correctly-shaped `(0, 3)` outputs. ## Assumptions and limitations - Field is cast to `float32` for the SDF; the QEF accumulators are `double` internally. - A `>= ~3-voxel` half-width band is required for a watertight result (e.g. from `rebuild_narrow_band(band=3)`). - Decimation (`reduce > 1` or `adaptivity > 0`) accumulates per-cluster QEFs with double `atomicAdd`, so decimated vertex positions are not bit-reproducible run to run; the decimation tests use count / validity / tolerance assertions rather than exact equality. ## Follow-ups - **Cached box-stencil resolver (AcademySoftwareFoundation/openvdb#2263).** The gather kernel resolves its 3×3×3 stencil with `computeBoxStencil`: 27 root-down tree walks per voxel, materialized into a 27-entry array. That is the baseline in #2263's measurements, where `forEachBoxStencilCached` (shared-memory per-leaf neighbour table, streamed taps) is 2.2× faster at block width 128. The gather already launches one 128-thread CUDA block per VBM block, the shape the cached resolvers use, and each block's grid is uniform. Adopting it means keeping the tail slots in the block-wide staging rather than returning early. This PR does not wait on #2263: the switch can follow once it merges and fVDB's NanoVDB pin moves past it. - **Upstream to NanoVDB (AcademySoftwareFoundation/openvdb#2441).** This op's mesher is proposed as `nanovdb::tools::cuda::DualContour`, along with batched meshing through a `VoxelBlockManagerBatchView`, decimation and a vertex-transform hook. Once it merges and the pin moves past it, `DualContour.cu` becomes a thin wrapper that keeps only the torch/JaggedTensor glue. A prototype of that wrapper gives bit-for-bit identical vertices and triangles (normals within 1 ulp) and is 1.3-2.1x faster than this PR, with fewer launches and syncs. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
